title: Regex runs on a linear-time engine by default; backtracking is opt-in and budgeted
scope:
which regular-expression engine `Core\Regex` uses, when the backtracking engine is reached,
what happens when its budget is exhausted, and which patterns are refused. Not in scope: the `Core\Regex`
method roster, which M8 designs.

summary.headline: Regular expressions run in linear time unless a pattern needs backtracking
summary.body:
`Core\Regex` runs on an engine that cannot be made to blow up: matching time grows linearly with
the input. Patterns that need lookaround or backreferences run on a second, backtracking engine
under a step budget, and exhausting the budget throws. PHP's equivalent limit makes `preg_match`
return `false`, a value almost nobody checks, so its denial-of-service guard becomes a wrong
answer. When the pattern is a literal, which engine it needs is known while building, so `nvs
check` can report a backtracking pattern on a request path.
